results.title: GPU rental without hyperscalers: How good are neo clouds?
highlights:
At Lambda, an H100 GPU costs 3.55 euros an hour, against 10.95 euros at Azure, according to the price list of 4 October 2026. Neo clouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Lambda offer another option alongside hyperscalers. Several providers expand using secured loans. CoreWeave depends on a few large customers for much of its revenue.

...

- Neo clouds rent out primarily GPU compute time, and on the list prices for an H100 hour they sit well below AWS and Azure, though Nebius raised its H100 hourly rate by 17 percent on 1 October 2026.
- As of 30 June 2026, CoreWeave carried debt equivalent to 31.24 billion euros, and Microsoft accounted for roughly 67 percent of CoreWeave’s revenue in 2025.
- European capacity is being created at Telekom in Munich, at Nebius in Finland and France, and in up to seven planned EU gigafactories.

...

For an hour on an Nvidia H100 GPU, the range on 4 October 2026 is wide. The rates are only comparable to a limited extent. Lambda charges the equivalent of 3.55 euros for the H100 SXM, calculated at the European Central Bank (ECB) reference rate of 2 October 2026. Nebius has been charging the equivalent of 4.01 euros since 1 October 2026, and CoreWeave charges the equivalent of 43.87 euros for a node with eight H100s, which works out at 5.48 euros per GPU. In the US East region, AWS charges the equivalent of 6.13 euros per GPU hour for the p5.48xlarge instance with eight H100s, according to the price tracker Vantage as of 3 October 2026. For the Azure VM ND96isr H100 v5, AzureSpeed lists the equivalent of 10.95 euros per GPU hour as of 26 September 2026 for Linux with usage-based billing in East US.

...

On 1 October 2026, Nebius raised the H100 hour from the equivalent of 3.43 to 4.01 euros, and the B200 from 6.37 to 7.57 euros. On 17 September 2026, CoreWeave reported short-duration contracts of three to six months at roughly 36 million euros in revenue per megawatt per year.

results.title: "AI compute gets cheaper every year" stopped being true on October 1. | Aslam Ahamed
highlights:
**Aslam Ahamed**: Head of IT | AI & Automation Leader — 32 AI agents in production | Odoo ERP & Enterprise Systems | Cloud (AWS, Azure, M365) | Digital Transformation in Real Estate | MBA.

---

"AI compute gets cheaper every year" stopped being true on October 1.

That day, Nebius put a new on-demand rate card into effect. Not a promo ending. A higher price for the same hardware.

1. H100 went from $3.85 to $4.50 per GPU-hour. That's +17%, about $468 a month for one GPU running around the clock. An 8-GPU node now costs $3,744 more per month for the same work.

2. The newest chips took the biggest hit. B300 rose 21% ($7.85 to $9.50). H200 +20%. B200 +19%. The scarcer the hardware, the steeper the hike.

3. The biggest jump wasn't a GPU at all. Memory-backed instances went up 41%. If you serve long-context models, run vector databases or RAG pipelines, your bill may track that number, not the GPU headline.

4. The "boring" parts moved too. AMD EPYC Genoa CPU capacity rose 25%. Nothing in the stack is a commodity line item anymore.

5. It's the second hike this year. In May, on-demand rose an average of 29% and spot 51%. This time customers got about two weeks' notice.

6. The market cheered. Nebius shares jumped as much as 11% pre-market on the news. Investors read higher prices as proof that demand still outruns supply.

results.title: Nebius erhöht GPU-Preise und treibt Ausbau mit KI-Infrastruktur
highlights:
LAPPEENRANTA / LONDON (IT BOLTWISE) – Nebius erhöht die Stundensätze für seine NVIDIA-GPUs spürbar und signalisiert damit Knappheit bei Rechenleistung. Im Jahresvergleich wächst der Quartalsumsatz laut Angaben aus den Geschäftszahlen um 454 Prozent, während parallel 5,66 Milliarden US-Dollar in Sachanlagen fließen. Für den Ausbau plant das Management ein neues Rechenzentrum mit bis zu 310 Megawatt und einem Projektvolumen von über 10 Milliarden US-Dollar. Mit der geplanten Integration von Inferize in die Plattform Token Factory will der Cloud-Anbieter außerdem die Inferenz-Performance von Modellstarts beschleunigen.

...

Technisch und betriebswirtschaftlich lässt sich der Schritt über konkrete Mietpreise fassen. Für den weit verbreiteten H100 hebt Nebius den On-Demand-Preis je Stunde von 3,85 auf 4,50 US-Dollar an. Bei Spitzenmodellen wie dem B300 nennt der Bericht sogar Aufschläge von bis zu 21 Prozent. In einem Umfeld, in dem viele Kunden angesichts früherer Zyklen zeitweise sinkende GPU-Mietpreise erwartet haben, ist das Signal klar: Der Bedarf an Rechenleistung folgt aktuell nicht linear dem Angebot. Damit rückt Nebius als Plattformanbieter stärker in Richtung eines Betreibers mit echter Preissetzungsmacht, nicht nur eines Commodity-Vermieters.

Die Preiserhöhung bleibt aber nicht isoliert, sondern wird im Bericht strategisch mit einer Software-Offensive verknüpft. Nebius habe den Zukauf von Inferize angekündigt, einem Startup, das auf Inferenz-Optimierung spezialisiert ist. Die Integration in die unternehmenseigene Plattform Token Factory soll Modellstarts beschleunigen, also genau dort ansetzen, wo viele Teams in der Praxis Zeit verlieren: beim Übergang vom trainierten Modell hin zur produktiven Ausführung, bei der Optimierung von Laufzeitpfaden, Batch-Strategien und Auslastung. Für Unternehmen heißt das: Wenn die Software-Schicht Effizienzgewinne bringt, können sich Kunden länger an den Anbieter binden, weil Architekturentscheidungen und Betriebsabläufe nicht in kurzer Zeit ausgetauscht werden.

results.title: Compute Futures Go Live: What the First GPU-Hour Price Curve Says About the AI Buildout — newscms
highlights:
On October 5, 2026, a commodity that has never been traded anywhere starts trading. The New York Mercantile Exchange, the clearing arm of CME Group, begins listing two futures contracts tied to the hourly rental price…

...

## Introduction

On October 5, 2026, a commodity that has never been traded anywhere starts trading. The New York Mercantile Exchange, the clearing arm of CME Group, begins listing two futures contracts tied to the hourly rental price of a single AI accelerator: the Nvidia H100, the chip at the center of the current training and inference economy, and the Blackwell-generation B200 that is displacing it.

The contracts are financially settled, so no GPU changes hands. Each one covers 730 GPU-hours — one accelerator for roughly one average month — and settles against a daily index published by Silicon Data, a benchmarking firm backed by the trading firm DRW. They are the H100 and B200 rental index futures, announced in August by CME Group and Silicon Data together and listed on NYMEX pending CFTC review.

This is a small story about market plumbing with a very large implication. For four years, the companies building the AI economy bought their central input by bilateral negotiation: a startup signed a quote with a neocloud, a hyperscaler negotiated a reserved cluster, an AI lab locked in multi-year capacity through a direct commercial relationship. Nobody had a public number to check that price against. As Silicon Data's chief executive Carmen Li put it when the contracts were announced, "two companies buying the exact same GPU capacity could pay wildly different prices with no way to know who got the better deal."

...

## The Curve Is Backwardated, and That Is the Real Headline

The B200 rental index, SDB200RT, entered September at $5.62 per GPU-hour, up 27.6% year to date. On September 7 the spot reading was $5.69. Committing to the same chip for a term cost less at every tenor: $5.73 for three months, $5.64 for six, and $5.39 for twelve. The market's forward rate — the price of a B200-hour at a future date, rather than a contract running to that date — sat at $5.68 three months out, $5.41 at six months, and $5.03 at twelve.

A curve shaped that way is called backwardated. Locking in a year of Blackwell capacity costs roughly 5% less per hour than renting spot today, and the twelve-month forward sits about 12% under the current index. Silicon Data is careful, correctly, to say this establishes what commitment costs now rather than what rates will do next summer. It is a quote, not a forecast. But it is the market's actual clearing price for the forward, and it points in one direction.

...

The most recent readings reinforce the sense of stabilization rather than spike. The B200 index stood at $5.45 per GPU-hour on the portal, and the H100 neo-cloud index at $2.53. August was the quietest full month in the B200 series since it began in August 2025: every daily value sat between $5.58 and $5.69, a spread of 2.0%, with no day moving more than 1.2%. Annualized volatility ran at 7.1%, the lowest month of 2026 and roughly a quarter of July's. In July, by contrast, the same index ranged from $5.62 to $6.01 with monthly moves of tens of cents.

...

The other thing the indices make measurable is how the chip generations price against each other. On July 27 the B200 index stood at $5.66 against an H100 neo-cloud rate of $2.75 — a premium of roughly 106%. On September 7 the portal showed B200 at $5.69 against H200 at $3.29 and H100 at $2.63, putting Blackwell at about 1.7 times the H200 and 2.2 times the H100.

A newer generation renting at about twice the prior one, holding that ratio through an entire summer, looks less like a launch premium that decays and more like a structural spread the market has settled on.

The same pattern shows up one rung down the ladder. Between early May and late July, the H200 neo-cloud rate rose 14.4%, from $2.70 to $3.09 per hour, while the H100 rose 7.0%. The premium between them spent May in the mid-single digits, collapsed to essentially nothing for a single day in mid-June when the two chips briefly rented for the same money, then re-rated to an average of 12.1% in July and peaked at 16.2%. Both rates rose; the H200 simply rose twice as much.

...

The honest caveat is in the data itself: daily changes in the two series were essentially uncorrelated over the twelve-week window, so there is no support yet for claims that the rates move together. And a young index can widen as its provider panel matures. What is established is the level, the direction, and the size of the spread. Watching it monthly is now a public exercise rather than a private negotiation.

...

Each contract represents a month's rent for one accelerator and settles financially against the Silicon Data index. No hardware moves. The B200 contract lists under the code GPU2 alongside the H100. CME Group was explicit that the products were announced pending CFTC review, so the launch itself carries regulatory contingency, and the first real volume will tell you how much of this is a commercial necessity versus a headline.

results.title: H100 Price per Hour in 2026: $1.25 to $11.07 | Opengrid
highlights:
The H100 price per hour depends almost entirely on who you rent it from. On 19 September 2026, on-demand list prices for the same NVIDIA H100 ranged from $1.25 to $11.07 per GPU-hour across twelve providers we looked at, according to getdeploying.com. That is a gap of nearly 9× for the same chip.

This post breaks down where those prices sit, why they split into three bands, and how contract and spot pricing change the picture.

A note on dates: every price here is a snapshot. On-demand list prices are from getdeploying.com on 19 Sep 2026, and SKUs vary by provider (interconnect, memory, node size). GPU prices move by double digits in weeks, so treat these numbers as a guide to the shape of the market, not a quote.

## H100 on-demand prices by provider

| Provider | Tier | H100 on-demand, $ per GPU-hour |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Google Cloud | Hyperscaler | $11.07 |
| Oracle | Hyperscaler | $10.00 |
| Azure | Hyperscaler | $6.98 |
| AWS | Hyperscaler | $6.88 |
| CoreWeave | Neocloud | $6.16 |
| Crusoe | Neocloud | $3.90 |
| Nebius | Neocloud | $3.85 |
| Lambda | Neocloud | $3.29 |
| RunPod | Developer cloud / marketplace | $2.89 |
| Together | Developer cloud / marketplace | $1.99 |
| Vast.ai | Developer cloud / marketplace | $1.79 |
| Lium | Developer cloud / marketplace | $1.25 |

Source: getdeploying.com, 19 Sep 2026. On-demand list prices. SKUs vary by provider.

...

Google Cloud, Oracle, Azure and AWS charge the most. You are paying for the rest of the platform around the GPU: the storage, networking, identity, compliance and enterprise contracts your company may already run on. For teams already deep inside one of these clouds, staying put can be worth the premium. For a training run that only needs GPUs, it often is not.

### Neoclouds: $3.29 to $6.16

CoreWeave, Crusoe, Nebius and Lambda are GPU-first clouds. They are built around AI workloads and price well below the hyperscalers, though the spread inside this tier is still almost 2×.

### Developer clouds and marketplaces: $1.25 to $2.89

RunPod, Together, Vast.ai and Lium sit at the bottom of the range. Some are developer clouds, some are marketplaces where many hosts list capacity. The prices are the lowest, and the trade-offs vary a lot from one provider to the next: availability, network setup, and how reliable a given host is.

## H100 vs other GPUs: the price bands

The H100 is not the only chip with a wide spread. Thunder Compute's September 2026 data shows the same pattern across the A100, H200 and B200:

| GPU | Price range, $ per hour |
| --- | --- |
| A100 | $1.09 to $5.07 |
| H100 | $2.89 to $11.06 |
| H200 | $3.44 to $10.60 |
| B200 | $3.50 to $27.04 |

Source: Thunder Compute, Sep 2026.

You may notice the H100 low end here ($2.89) is higher than the $1.25 in the provider table above. The two come from different sources, on different dates, covering different sets of providers. They don't contradict each other. They show that the answer to "what does an H100 cost?" depends on whose list you check and when.

Each GPU type also moves on its own. During one stretch, H100 rental prices rose 10% while A100 and B200 stayed flat. The cheapest chip for your job this month is not guaranteed to be the cheapest next month.

...

On-demand list prices are only one of three ways to pay.

| Pricing tier | What it means | What happened to H100 pricing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On-demand | Pay by the hour, no commitment | $1.25 to $11.07 depending on provider (getdeploying.com, 19 Sep 2026) |
| One-year contract | Commit for a year in exchange for a lower rate | Rose from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between Oct 2025 and Mar 2026, about +40% (SemiAnalysis) |
| Spot | Spare capacity at a discount, can be pulled mid-job | Runs 60% to 91% below on-demand |

...

## Why H100 prices differ so much

A few forces keep the spread wide:

- The market is fragmented. SemiAnalysis tracks 209 GPU clouds. Each has its own console, contract and API, so comparing them all by hand is impractical.
- Capacity is tight. SemiAnalysis reported on-demand sold out across all GPU types in 2026, and Thunder Compute reports most new NVIDIA allocation is reserved into 2027. When cheap capacity disappears, buyers pay whatever is available.
- Prices move fast. AWS cut its H100 on-demand price by 44% in a single announcement in June 2025. A few months later, contract prices were up 40%. See how GPU rental prices moved in 2025 and 2026.
- Switching is expensive. Moving to a cheaper provider means a new account, a new contract, a new API and a new bill. So most teams pick once and stay, even after their provider stops being the best deal.

results.title: GPU Rental Prices 2025-2026: How Fast They Move | Opengrid
highlights:
## The short version

| When | What happened | Move | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 5 Jun 2025 | AWS cuts its H100 on-demand price in a single announcement | −44% | AWS, via CloudZero and IntuitionLabs |
| Jun to Jul 2025 | Other providers follow with their own cuts, in single moves | −20% to −25% | CloudZero, IntuitionLabs |
| Oct 2025 to Mar 2026 | One-year H100 contract price climbs from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour | about +40% | SemiAnalysis |
| Dec 2025 to Jan 2026 | Silicon Data H100 rental index rises from $2.00 to $2.20 in four weeks | +10% | Silicon Data |
| 2026 | On-demand capacity sold out across all GPU types | n/a | SemiAnalysis |

In fifteen months the H100 went from a sharp price war to a shortage, with prices rising again.

## Mid-2025: the price war

On 5 June 2025, AWS cut its H100 on-demand price by 44% in a single announcement. That is not a gradual drift. It is nearly half the price, overnight, from the largest cloud provider in the world.

Other providers did not wait long. Through June and July 2025, several cut their own prices by 20% to 25%, again in single moves rather than small steps.

For buyers, this was the moment to renegotiate or move. Teams that had signed earlier contracts, or picked a provider and stayed put, kept paying the old price.

## Late 2025 into 2026: the reversal

Then the direction flipped.

- Contract prices rose about 40%. SemiAnalysis tracked one-year H100 contracts rising from $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October 2025 and March 2026.
- The rental index jumped 10% in four weeks. Silicon Data's H100 rental index went from $2.00 to $2.20 between December 2025 and January 2026.
- Capacity dried up. SemiAnalysis reported on-demand sold out across all GPU types in 2026, and Thunder Compute reports most new NVIDIA allocation is reserved into 2027.

The teams that locked in contracts at the low point did well. The teams that waited paid 40% more for the same commitment a few months later.

## Each GPU moves on its own

It is tempting to think of "GPU prices" as one number. They are not. During the same stretch where the H100 rental index rose 10%, A100 and B200 prices stayed flat (Silicon Data).

Every GPU type has its own price band, and the bands are wide. Thunder Compute's September 2026 data:

| GPU | Price range, $ per hour |
| --- | --- |
| A100 | $1.09 to $5.07 |
| H100 | $2.89 to $11.06 |
| H200 | $3.44 to $10.60 |
| B200 | $3.50 to $27.04 |

Source: Thunder Compute, Sep 2026.

So "is now a good time to rent?" has no single answer. It depends on the chip, the provider and the pricing tier. For a provider-by-provider breakdown, see H100 price per hour in 2026.

results.title: Neoclouds explained: the GPU cloud providers | BlockWest Learn
highlights:
A neocloud is a cloud company built specifically to rent out AI computing power, mostly Nvidia GPUs (graphics processing units, the chips used to train and run AI models). Unlike Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure or Google Cloud, which sell hundreds of services from storage to databases, neoclouds focus on large clusters of accelerators, fast networking between them, and the software to schedule AI workloads.

...

The core product is GPU rental, priced per GPU-hour (one chip running for one hour). Small customers pay on demand. The bulk of revenue, however, comes from large customers that reserve whole clusters for several years.

Those reservations are usually take-or-pay contracts: the customer commits to pay for the capacity whether or not it uses it. The contracts are what make the model financeable. A neocloud signs a multi-year commitment, then borrows against that contract and the GPUs it buys to fulfil it, and repays the debt from the customer’s payments.

The economics depend on three numbers: the price per GPU-hour, the share of capacity that is actually paid for (utilization), and how long the chips stay commercially useful. For reference, Silicon Data’s neocloud H100 rental index stood at $2.93 per GPU-hour on November 1, 2026. The H100 is Nvidia’s previous-generation flagship; newer Blackwell chips rent for more.

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Dataset
highlights: A free, openly licensed (CC BY 4.0) dataset of posted cloud GPU rental prices across the whole market: GPU marketplaces, specialized GPU clouds, serverless platforms and hyperscale clouds. It contains a normalized snapshot of every current posted offer (provider, GPU model, VRAM, offer type, region, per-GPU-hour price, minimum GPU count, availability) and a daily price series with each day's lowest, average and highest posted price per provider and GPU. Every price is a rate a provider publishes. None is a transaction. This version (2026-10-04) holds the snapshot of 2026-10-04 06:50 UTC and the daily series from 2026-08-05 to 2026-10-04. It is the first version to carry corrections: three labelling errors found on 2026-10-03 (a preemptible rate recorded as on-demand at one provider, a PCIe card recorded under the SXM name at two) are listed in corrections.json, the daily series is published both corrected (gpu-prices-daily) and exactly as recorded (gpu-prices-daily-as-recorded), and no assumed price is filled in. Earlier versions hold days back to 2026-07-31 and predate these corrections. It also archives FastGPU's comment to the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission on the Request for Comment on the Listing of Compute Derivatives Contracts (RIN 3038-AF77, 91 FR 54259), together with the script, inputs and output that reproduce every figure in that comment (cftc-rin-3038-AF77-replication.zip). Published and maintained by FastGPU, a live GPU price comparison service. Official dataset page and column documentation: https://fastgpu.co/dataset. Method: https://fastgpu.co/methodology.

results.title: How to Choose (and Switch) GPU Cloud Providers | Opengrid
highlights:
- 209 GPU clouds. SemiAnalysis tracks 209 GPU clouds, up from 124. Each has its own console, contract, API and bill.
- Prices spread across a wide band. An on-demand H100 lists from about $1.25 an hour at developer clouds and marketplaces to $11.07 an hour at the most expensive hyperscaler. The same is true of other chips: A100s range from $1.09 to $5.07 an hour and B200s from $3.50 to $27.04.
- Reliability varies a lot. SemiAnalysis's ClusterMAX 2.0 grades GPU clouds from Platinum down to Underperforming. Only one is rated Platinum.
- Capacity is tight. SemiAnalysis reported in 2026 that on-demand capacity was sold out across all GPU types, and Thunder Compute reports most new NVIDIA allocation is reserved into 2027.

...

So teams pick once and overpay for as long as they stay. That made sense when prices barely moved. It makes less sense now. AWS cut its H100 on-demand price by 44% in a single announcement in June 2025. Then one-year H100 contract prices rose about 40% between October 2025 and March 2026. The right provider this quarter is often the wrong one next quarter. More on that in how GPU rental prices moved in 2025 and 2026.

...

### 3. Benchmark the price against the market
